name: Ideal transformer
seoDesc: Ideal transformer: work out primary voltage from the primary windings and the secondary windings. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: Supply the primary windings, the secondary windings, the secondary voltage and the primary current and the Ideal transformer calculator solves for primary voltage. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Ideal transformer calculator work?
sections.html:
The Ideal transformer calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports primary voltage in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the primary windings, the secondary windings, the secondary voltage and the primary current.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in amperes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Ideal transformer calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Primary voltage=primary windings × secondary voltage ÷ secondary windings
Secondary current=primary current × primary windings ÷ secondary windings

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Primary windings = 10, Secondary windings = 10 and Secondary voltage = 10 V. Working through the relationship above gives Primary voltage = 10 V.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Primary voltage = 10 V should be roughly the size you expected from Primary windings = 10 and Secondary windings = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in volts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in amperes, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Ideal transformer calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the primary windings, the secondary windings and the secondary voltage — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Ideal transformer calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns primary voltage, derived from the primary windings, the secondary windings and the secondary voltage. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Ideal transformer calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the primary windings, the secondary windings, the secondary voltage and the primary current, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter primary voltage in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Primary voltage opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Primary voltage = 10 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Ideal transformer calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
